justification:
Technical round 1 review of /oop-design/dependency-injection/, read fresh from the issue-112 worktree (src/content/articles/oop-design/dependency-injection.md; no docs/crosslinks file exists for this slug yet, which is fine at round 1 with no cut siblings referenced). `node tools/run-code.mjs` against the worktree file: PASS, blocks=18, executed=9 - every one of the nine runnable programs, including the MiniContainer demo, the real-MSDI equivalent, the captive-dependency demo, the ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild failure, and the IServiceScopeFactory fix, compiled and produced exactly the output block printed in the article.

Item 1 (hand-trace the ~60-line MiniContainer against the four-type diamond, all three lifetimes): traced `Resolve`/`ResolveSingleton`/`ResolveScoped`/`Create`/`CreateScope` by hand rather than trusting the compiler. `CreateScope()` returns a new `MiniContainer` sharing the same `_registrations` dictionary (so `Registration` objects, and therefore cached `SingletonInstance` fields, are shared across every scope and the root) but with a fresh, private `_scoped` dictionary per scope. `ResolveScoped` caches in the *calling* container's own `_scoped`, so two resolutions inside one `using var scope1` share one `ConsoleAuditLog` while a second `CreateScope()` gets a different one. `ResolveSingleton` always resolves through `_root ?? this`, so `SystemClock` is built exactly once and is reached identically through both paths of the diamond (directly by `InvoiceService` and indirectly through `IAuditLog`/`IReceiptSender`). Hand-tracing scope1's two resolves and scope2's one resolve reproduces all four printed booleans exactly: same audit log within scope1 (True), different audit log across scopes (False), different transient `SmtpReceiptSender` within scope1 (False), and one shared `SystemClock` instance reachable from every path (True). This matches the article's claimed output and the real `dotnet run` output confirmed by run-code. The container genuinely implements all three lifetimes correctly, not just superficially.

Item 2 (captive dependency: singleton IReceiptSender capturing scoped IAuditLog, `[audit #1]` printed for both scopes): confirmed both by hand-trace and by the actual run-code pass. `SmtpReceiptSender` is registered singleton, so `ResolveSingleton`/the real container's equivalent builds it once, on the first ask, resolving its `IAuditLog` constructor parameter from that one build - not re-resolved per scope. `scope2`'s `InvoiceService.Process` call therefore drives the *same*, already-frozen `SmtpReceiptSender`, still holding `ConsoleAuditLog` instance #1 from scope1. The claimed output ([audit #1] for INV-4001, [audit #1] again for INV-4002) is exactly what a real .NET container does with this registration and was independently reproduced by the run-code execution. Central gotcha is correct.

Item 3 (ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild exception message): the demo throws and unwraps an `AggregateException` down to the innermost exception and prints 'Cannot consume scoped service 'IAuditLog' from singleton 'IReceiptSender'.' - run-code confirms this is the real output of the real package, not an invented string. Checked against Microsoft's own guidelines page (`dependency-injection/guidelines`), which documents this exact anti-pattern with its own Foo/Bar example and states you get 'an InvalidOperationException with a message similar to "Cannot consume scoped service 'Bar' from singleton 'Foo'."' - identical message shape with the article's own type names substituted, exactly as the article claims ('the same message shape Microsoft's guidelines document ... reproduced here from a real run rather than copied from the page'). Plausible and accurate, and empirically verified rather than merely plausible.

Item 4 ('the singleton's scoped dependency is built from the container's own internal root context, not from whichever caller's scope triggered construction'): this specific phrasing is the article's own explanatory language, not presented as a direct Microsoft quote, and is not independently cited. It is, however, an accurate description of real Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection behavior (singletons are constructed once against the provider's root scope) and is consistent with everything Microsoft's own pages say about the effect: overview.md's scope-validation section (scoped services resolved from the root are 'effectively promoted to singleton'), service-lifetimes.md ('resolve a scoped service directly from a singleton ... causes the scoped service to behave like a singleton'), and guidelines.md's captive-dependency section, all describing the same externally-observable consequence this claim explains mechanically. The claim is also self-verified by the article's own two demos (MiniContainer's `ResolveSingleton` doing exactly this, and the real MSDI captive-dependency demo producing the predicted symptom). Accurate; not a fabrication, though it sits right at the edge of the 'every non-obvious factual claim has a primary source' rule since no citation marker is attached to that specific sentence - see issue below.

Item 5 (IServiceScopeFactory-always-singleton claim and the scope-factory fix pattern): verified verbatim against overview.md - 'The IServiceScopeFactory is always registered as a singleton' is an exact quote, correctly cited as [[1]]. The fix pattern shown (`ScopedReceiptSender(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory)`, `CreateScope()` + `GetRequiredService<IAuditLog>()` inside `Send`, `using` to dispose the scope) is a materially faithful, independently-written reproduction of the pattern overview.md itself recommends and demonstrates in its own BackgroundService/IServiceScopeFactory sample (not copied - different example, different domain). The demo's printed output ([audit #1] then [audit #2], one fresh scope and audit log per call) is correct given the pattern and was confirmed by run-code.

Item 6 (citation integrity, all 6 sources spot-checked - all 6, not just 3-4): all six fetched live and checked against the specific sentence each is cited on.
- [[1]] overview: hard-coded-dependency three costs paraphrase matches the source's three bullets (modify the class to replace the dependency; configuration of the dependency's own dependencies has to be threaded through; can't unit test without a real connection) without close paraphrase or copying. Constructor-injection terminology, IServiceScopeFactory-singleton quote, and the Development-environment scope-validation-by-default claim (via `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder`, matching the source's 'calls CreateApplicationBuilder to build the host') are all verbatim-accurate.
- [[2]] service-lifetimes: cited for 'the built-in container recognizes exactly three [lifetimes], and defines each one precisely' - correct: the page does define exactly three lifetimes in prose (transient/scoped/singleton sections), even though the article's exact quoted definitions are attributed to [[3]] a sentence later. No misattribution.
- [[3]] ServiceLifetime enum: all three quoted fragments - 'a new instance of the service will be created every time it is requested' (Transient), 'a new instance of the service will be created for each scope' (Scoped), 'a single instance of the service will be created' (Singleton) - are exact verbatim substrings of the live enum table's field descriptions.
- [[4]] guidelines: the captive-dependency definition and the Mark Seemann attribution match verbatim ('The term "captive dependency", coined by Mark Seemann ... refers to the misconfiguration of service lifetimes, where a longer-lived service holds a shorter-lived service captive.'). The closing thread-safety citation ('the container only guarantees that resolving services is thread-safe, not that the objects it hands back are') accurately paraphrases the page's own Thread safety section and its boxed note about resolved instances needing their own synchronization.
- [[5]] BuildServiceProvider: the quoted ValidateScopes description ('that scoped services never gets resolved from root provider') is a verbatim substring of that page's Boolean-overload parameter documentation, and the page does document a `BuildServiceProvider(IServiceCollection, ServiceProviderOptions)` overload as the article uses.
- [[6]] ServiceProviderOptions: the quoted ValidateOnBuild description ('indicates whether validation is performed to ensure all services can be created when BuildServiceProvider ... is called') is verbatim, with '...' correctly standing in for the elided overload signature.
No fabricated, misattributed, or unsupported-by-the-cited-page claims found across any of the six sources.

Not higher than 9.3: the article is essentially flawless technically - accurate, deep (covers all three lifetimes, a working hand-rolled container, the composition-root risk, the captive-dependency bug, validation, and the documented fix, each demonstrated with real, verified code rather than asserted), and every citation checked out. It is held just under a 9.5+ by the one uncited-but-true mechanical claim in item 4 and the very minor ValidateScopes attribution wording noted below - neither is a factual error, so neither caps the score, but a strict editor would want the item-4 sentence tied to a citation marker even though it is self-demonstrated by the code.

issues.location: 'The captive dependency: a singleton that outlives its scope' section, the sentence beginning "`SmtpReceiptSender` is a singleton, so the container builds it exactly once..."
issues.problem: The clause 'that one build resolved IAuditLog from the container's own internal root context rather than from either caller's scope' is an accurate description of real Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection behavior and is self-demonstrated by the article's own two working demos, but it carries no citation marker, unlike almost every other non-obvious claim on the page. It sits close to the line the brief draws ('every non-obvious factual claim has a primary source, fetched and read during research').
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite it to [[2]] (service-lifetimes.md's captive-dependency guidance) / [[4]] (guidelines.md's captive-dependency section), which together describe the same externally observable effect, or rephrase the sentence as the article's own inference from the demo's output ('the boolean above shows why: ...') rather than as a freestanding factual assertion.

issues.location: 'The captive dependency' section, the sentence "`BuildServiceProvider` has an overload that takes a `ServiceProviderOptions`, whose `ValidateScopes` property checks '...that scoped services never gets resolved from root provider'[[5]]"
issues.problem: The quoted phrase is verbatim, but it is actually the parameter documentation for the older `BuildServiceProvider(IServiceCollection, bool validateScopes)` overload on the cited [[5]] page, not the `ServiceProviderOptions.ValidateScopes` property's own documentation (which is worded slightly differently: 'ensure that scoped services are never resolved from the root provider', and lives on the page cited separately as [[6]]). The sentence's grammar attributes the quote to 'the ValidateScopes property', which is a small conflation of two documented members that happen to describe the same check.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either attribute the quote to the Boolean-overload parameter doc explicitly ('the validateScopes parameter of the older bool overload') or switch to quoting ServiceProviderOptions.ValidateScopes's own property description ('ensure that scoped services are never resolved from the root provider') and cite [[6]] instead of [[5]] for that clause.
